« Ce n’est pas une anomalie » – Réaction: “It’s not an anomaly” – Suspicious reactions on a post by the Immigration minister
Une vague de « likes » venus de profils: A wave of “likes” from dubious profiles abroad raises questions about the authenticity of the reactions to Minister Roberge’s post.
Jean-François Roberge, ministre de l’Imm: Jean-François Roberge, Minister of Immigration. Photo credit: La Converse montage
Cette enquête découle d’une curiosité to: This investigation grew out of a simple question: why would a local political post suddenly attract several thousand positive reactions, many of which seem to come from profiles located abroad?
Pour comprendre ce phénomène d’engagemen: To understand this unusual spike in engagement on a post by the Immigration minister, I worked with Belinda Kanga, our digital strategist. We manually analyzed a sample of 360 profiles, out of the just over 6,000 reactions the post had drawn. La Converse also consulted two independent computer scientists, who reached the same conclusions. This work cannot establish a definitive finding, but it brings out clear trends that help explain what happened.
Parallèlement, nous nous sommes entreten: We also spoke with Yacine Kraimia, the computer engineer who raised the alarm about the minister’s post, and with Bruno Guglielminetti, a digital communications specialist, who helped us place this phenomenon in the broader context of the authenticity of online engagement.
J’espère que cette enquête vous permettr: I hope this investigation will help you better understand the grey areas surrounding this type of digital activity.
La plus récente <l1>publication Facebook: The most recent <l1>Facebook post by Quebec Immigration Minister Jean-François Roberge</l1> generated an unusual volume of interactions: several thousand reactions, a significant proportion of which came from accounts located in the Philippines, Pakistan, Indonesia and other countries with no obvious connection to Quebec.
Plusieurs de ces profils semblent en out: Many of these profiles also look dubious – generic photos, no activity or newly created profiles – which raises questions about the possible existence of fake accounts and bots, as well as the use of artificial amplification tactics.
Cette vague d’engagement survient alors: This wave of engagement comes as the minister’s proposed reform, which would move from the Programme de l’expérience québécoise (PEQ) to the Programme de sélection des travailleurs qualifiés (PSTQ), has come under sharp criticism since it was announced. The reform is strongly opposed by several affected groups and has been poorly received by part of the Quebec population.
Dans ce contexte, la vague inhabituelle: In this context, the unusual wave of positive reactions to a recent post on the minister’s Facebook account – totalling more than 10,000 interactions – surprised many internet users, especially since Jean-François Roberge’s posts usually draw a few dozen reactions, and sometimes a few hundred at best.
La Converse a analysé un échantillon de: La Converse analyzed a sample of 360 Facebook accounts that reacted to this post. The results raise serious questions.
Selon une analyse réalisée à l’interne p: According to an in-house analysis by Belinda Kanga, digital strategist and data analyst at La Converse, the positive reactions – the “Like,” “Love” and “Care” reactions – are tied to engagement behaviours that raise serious doubts. They also show average suspicion scores that are markedly higher than those observed in the negative reactions. Conversely, the accounts that reacted with an angry emoji appear to be largely organic. They come from real, coherent, locally rooted profiles.
L’analyse, réalisée manuellement selon u: The analysis, carried out manually using an investigative approach, cannot state beyond all doubt that this engagement was purchased or organized. However, the trends identified point to a level of probability ranging from “high to very high.” The indicators observed – foreign profiles, languages irrelevant to a Quebec context, semi-inactive or locked accounts, inconsistent histories – match typical markers of “engagement farms,” which are linked to “purchased engagement.” La Converse also consulted two independent computer scientists who examined these suspicious reactions and reached the same conclusions.
Une « ferme à clics », aussi appelée « f: A “click farm,” also called an “engagement farm,” is a network of automated accounts (bots) or manually controlled accounts. It is used to artificially inflate engagement around a post. It generally consists of recent, semi-inactive or foreign-based profiles, mobilized to mass-produce “Likes,” reactions or positive comments. The purpose of using a click farm is to create an impression of popularity or support that does not necessarily reflect real public opinion.
« Je ne peux pas dire à 100 % que ces ré: “I can’t say with 100% certainty that these reactions are artificial, but the signals converge toward a high probability,” explains Belinda Kanga. “Two out of three reactions – and the most numerous – show characteristic signs of this type of activity.”
<strong>Deux scénarios possibles, selon: Two possible scenarios, according to an expert
Ce phénomène n’est pas totalement inédit: This phenomenon is not entirely new in Quebec. According to Bruno Guglielminetti, a digital communications specialist who is the producer and host of the podcast Mon Carnet, there are two possible scenarios when a political post suddenly receives a large volume of suspicious reactions.
« Quelqu’un au sein du gouvernement a eu: “Either someone within the government had the bad idea of buying a few thousand Likes, or someone in the opposition bought Likes on this post to make the government look bad. Unfortunately, it’s happened quite often,” he says.
Bruno Guglielminetti souligne également: Bruno Guglielminetti also points out that the massive arrival of reactions from fake profiles or accounts located abroad can “signal a distortion of public conversation.” In his view, this type of engagement skews the perception of how the message was actually received and “blurs the reading of public opinion,” since the local audience ends up drowned in outside noise that can be exploited.
Il rappelle que ce genre d’amplification: He notes that this kind of amplification can be used to “imitate popular support around a minister or a measure,” to “influence general perception,” or can “result from an opportunistic effect of automated account networks that exploit highly visible content.” In some cases, it can also come from organized actors seeking to weigh in on the political conversation.
Le spécialiste met en garde contre les r: The specialist warns of the risks of this practice: artificially inflated engagement can lead to “a loss of credibility, weaken trust in institutions and damage the integrity of the digital public space.” He notes that it also fuels widespread scepticism toward engagement signals, even when they are authentic.
Contacté par La Converse, le cabinet du: Contacted by La Converse, Minister Jean-François Roberge’s office says it has noticed this “anomaly.” In a statement sent by email to our newsroom, the minister also rejects the idea that he is behind the increase in reactions: “To allege that we are behind the sudden rise in reactions is completely wrong.”
Par ailleurs, M. Roberge rejette aussi l: Mr. Roberge also rejects the idea that money was spent on such an operation. “No money was used to buy visibility or reactions on this post. That is not how we operate,” the same statement reads. Finally, his office says internal checks are under way “to understand the impact of the situation, notably on the reach of our future posts.”
<strong>« Ce n’est pas une anomalie », r: “It’s not an anomaly,” responds the whistleblower
De son côté, Yacine Kraimia, l’informati: For his part, Yacine Kraimia, the computer engineer who raised the alarm about the bots, considers that this is not an anomaly but a fact. “I’m not saying it’s the minister or someone in his office who did it, but it’s not a mistake, it’s not an anomaly as the minister said, it’s something that was done, someone did it,” he insists in an interview with La Converse.
Se fondant sur son expertise, M. Kraimia: Drawing on his expertise, Mr. Kraimia analyzed hundreds of reactions before noticing this dubious spike. Calling the affair a “scandal,” he called out the minister last Tuesday, before alerting the media to the use of bots or fake profiles on the Facebook page of Immigration Minister Jean-François Roberge. “Using this type of tactic to artificially inflate the perception of public support is not only misleading, but also deeply shameful for a government institution,” he wrote at the time.
Cette situation survient dans un context: This situation comes at a time when debates around immigration are particularly sensitive in Quebec. The gap between the climate of opposition to the shift from the PEQ to the PSTQ and the wave of positive reactions to this post surprised many internet users. The strong presence of accounts located abroad makes the phenomenon all the more surprising.
Comme le souligne également Bruno Guglie: As Bruno Guglielminetti also points out, there are “a few tools” to detect inauthentic behaviour, but no standardized public benchmark currently makes it possible to clearly confirm or rule out the real origin of this type of engagement. The platforms’ internal mechanisms remain “not very transparent,” leaving these situations in a grey zone that is hard to interpret. In a context where migration debates are charged, this affair leaves an open question: how can we guarantee that signals of political engagement still reflect something real? It is a democratic issue in its own right.
